Threat actor taxonomy
Which actor is driven mainly by ideology or political causes?
Hacktivists
Cybercriminal groups
Malicious insiders
Ransomware affiliates
Hacktivists attack to make a political or social statement, often through defacement, leaks or DDoS.
d
Threat actor taxonomy
Why do defenders profile threat actors' motivation and capability?
To prioritise defences against the actors most likely to target them
To identify and arrest every attacker personally
To decide which actors are legally allowed to attack
To replace the need for vulnerability management
Understanding who is likely to attack, and how, guides investment and detection.
m
Malware types
What distinguishes a worm from a virus?
A worm spreads by itself across networks; a virus needs a host file or user action
A worm infects only Linux; a virus infects only Windows
A worm encrypts files; a virus steals passwords
A worm is legal software; a virus is illegal software
Worms self-propagate, as WannaCry did; viruses attach to hosts and rely on execution.
m
Malware types
What is a Trojan?
Malware disguised as legitimate software
Malware that only spreads over Wi-Fi
A tool that blocks malicious websites
A patch that fixes a vulnerability
Trojans rely on users trusting and running them.
d
Malware types
Why is fileless malware hard for signature-based antivirus to detect?
It runs in memory using legitimate tools, leaving few files to scan
It uses files too large for antivirus engines to open
It deletes the antivirus program before running
It only runs on computers without hard disks
Living-off-the-land techniques abuse tools like PowerShell; behaviour-based detection is needed.
m
Ransomware
What is double extortion in ransomware attacks?
Encrypting data and threatening to leak stolen copies
Demanding two payments from the same bank account
Encrypting data twice with two different keys
Attacking two companies with the same malware
Data theft before encryption adds leak pressure even if backups allow recovery.
m
Social engineering
What is spear phishing?
Phishing tailored to a specific person or organisation
Phishing sent to millions of random addresses
Phishing carried out only by telephone
Phishing that targets fishing companies
Spear phishing uses research on the target to appear credible.
m
Social engineering
What is whaling?
Phishing aimed at senior executives
Phishing sent through SMS messages
Mass phishing with misspelled emails
Phishing that uses QR codes
Whaling targets high-value individuals such as CEOs and finance heads.
d
Social engineering
An email from the 'CEO' urgently asks finance to wire money before a deadline. Which psychological trigger is used?
Authority combined with urgency
Reciprocity combined with liking
Scarcity combined with curiosity
Consensus combined with boredom
BEC attacks combine perceived authority with time pressure to bypass normal checks.
d
Social engineering
Which control best defeats business email compromise payment fraud?
Verifying payment changes through a separate, known channel
Asking staff to reply to the email to confirm it is genuine
Blocking all emails that contain attachments
Using a longer email signature for executives
Out-of-band verification breaks the attacker's control of the conversation.
m
Social engineering
What is vishing?
Voice phishing by telephone
Phishing through video calls only
Phishing via visual ads
Virus-based phishing
Vishing uses phone calls; smishing uses SMS.
d
Email authentication
What do SPF, DKIM and DMARC help prevent?
Spoofing of an organisation's email domain
Malware hidden inside encrypted attachments
Users clicking links in genuine emails
Mail servers running out of storage
These standards let receivers verify a sender is authorised for the domain and apply a policy to failures.
m
DoS and DDoS
What is the difference between DoS and DDoS?
DDoS uses many distributed sources, such as a botnet
DDoS targets data; DoS targets only hardware
DoS is illegal while DDoS is a testing method
DDoS affects confidentiality; DoS affects integrity
Distributed attacks come from many machines, making them harder to block.
m
DDoS categories
A SYN flood exhausts a server's connection table. Which category of DDoS is this?
Protocol (state-exhaustion) attack
Volumetric bandwidth attack
Application-layer attack
Physical-layer attack
SYN floods abuse the TCP handshake to fill connection state; volumetric attacks saturate bandwidth.
d
DDoS categories
Why are application-layer (Layer 7) DDoS attacks harder to filter?
Their requests look like legitimate user traffic
They use more bandwidth than any other type
They only target DNS servers on port 53
They can be stopped only by unplugging the server
HTTP floods mimic real requests, so simple volume or protocol filters do not separate them.
d
DDoS mitigation
How do scrubbing centres and anycast help mitigate DDoS?
They spread and filter attack traffic before it reaches the target
They encrypt traffic so attackers cannot read it
They block all traffic from foreign countries
They create backups of the attacked website
Anycast distributes load across sites; scrubbing removes malicious traffic upstream.
m
Botnets
How did the Mirai botnet recruit devices?
By logging in to IoT devices with default credentials
By exploiting a flaw in desktop web browsers
By sending infected USB drives by post
By compromising certificate authorities
Mirai scanned for devices using factory-default usernames and passwords.
m
Threat intelligence
What turns raw data into threat intelligence?
Collection, processing and analysis that produce actionable insight
Storing large volumes of logs on a central server
Buying a commercial threat feed of IP addresses
Encrypting the data before sharing it
Intelligence is analysed and contextualised; raw indicators alone are data.
m
Threat intelligence levels
Which level of threat intelligence is aimed at executives and boards?
Strategic
Technical
Tactical
Operational
Strategic intelligence covers trends and business risk in non-technical language.
d
Intelligence lifecycle
Which phase starts the threat intelligence lifecycle?
Planning and direction
Dissemination
Processing
Feedback
Requirements set in planning and direction decide what to collect and why.
d
Pyramid of Pain
According to the Pyramid of Pain, which indicators cause attackers the most difficulty when defenders detect them?
Tactics, techniques and procedures (TTPs)
File hash values
IP addresses
Domain names
Changing behaviour is costly; changing a hash or IP is trivial.
m
OSINT
What is passive reconnaissance in OSINT?
Gathering information without sending traffic to the target's systems
Scanning the target's servers with a port scanner
Sending phishing emails to the target's staff
Logging in to the target's systems with found credentials
Passive methods use third-party sources such as search engines, WHOIS and public records.
d
OSINT ethics
Why should a defender avoid uploading confidential internal documents to public multi-scanner services?
Uploaded files may become available to other users of the service
Public scanners delete the original file from the uploader's computer
Uploading files is illegal under every national law
Scanners always mark internal documents as malware
Some services share submissions with subscribers, which can leak sensitive data.
m
MITRE ATT&CK
What is the MITRE ATT&CK framework?
A knowledge base of adversary tactics and techniques from real-world observations
A government law that defines cyber offences
A firewall product sold by MITRE
A checklist for passing ISO 27001 audits
ATT&CK catalogues behaviour by tactic (the why) and technique (the how).
d
MITRE ATT&CK
In ATT&CK, what is the difference between a tactic and a technique?
A tactic is the adversary's goal; a technique is how they achieve it
A tactic is a tool; a technique is the attacker's group name
A tactic is a defensive control; a technique is an exploit
They are two names for the same column in the matrix
For example, Credential Access is a tactic; OS Credential Dumping is a technique.
m
MITRE ATT&CK
How many tactics does the ATT&CK Enterprise matrix list?
The Enterprise matrix has 14 tactics, from Reconnaissance to Impact.
d
ATT&CK coverage
How do defenders use ATT&CK to find gaps?
By mapping existing detections to techniques and seeing which are uncovered
By counting how many vendors they buy tools from
By measuring the bandwidth of their internet connection
By listing which employees have attended training
Coverage maps show where detection and prevention are missing for relevant techniques.
m
Threat reports
Which section of a threat report should a busy executive read first?
The executive summary
The technical appendix
The IoC list
The raw log extracts
The executive summary states the key findings, impact and recommended actions in plain language.
d
Threat reports
Why should a threat report separate facts from assessments?
Readers need to know what was observed versus what is judged likely
Facts must always be written in a different language
Assessments are not allowed in professional reports
Facts are secret, so they go in a separate document
Clear labelling, often with confidence levels, prevents speculation being mistaken for evidence.
m
Threat reports
What makes a threat report actionable?
Specific recommendations and indicators that defenders can apply
A long history of every attacker group ever reported
A large number of charts and colourful diagrams
Technical jargon that shows the author's expertise
Actionable reports tell each audience what to do next.
